questions.stem: A student covers part of a leaf with aluminium foil, leaves the plant in light for 24 hours, then tests the leaf for starch with iodine. What result would they expect?

options.text: The whole leaf turns blue-black
Only the uncovered part turns blue-black; the covered part stays brown
Only the covered part turns blue-black
The whole leaf stays brown

questions.explanation: The uncovered part of the leaf receives light and can photosynthesise, producing glucose that is stored as starch (positive iodine test: blue-black). The covered part receives no light, so no photosynthesis occurs and no starch is produced (negative iodine test: stays brown/yellow). This demonstrates that light is required for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: Before testing a leaf for starch, a student places the plant in darkness for 48 hours. Why is this destarching step necessary?

options.text: To kill the plant so the experiment is safe
To remove any existing starch so that only newly produced starch during the experiment is detected
To increase the rate of photosynthesis
To make the leaves turn white

questions.explanation: Destarching ensures the leaf starts the experiment with no starch. Any starch detected after the experiment must have been produced during the experimental period. Without destarching, starch already present from previous photosynthesis would give a false positive result.

questions.stem: In the pondweed bubble experiment, a student counts bubbles of oxygen at different light intensities. They find that doubling the light intensity initially doubles the bubble count, but eventually increasing light has no effect. What limits the rate at very high light intensities?

options.text: The water becomes too warm
Another factor such as CO2 concentration or temperature becomes the limiting factor
The plant runs out of chlorophyll
Oxygen inhibits photosynthesis at high concentrations

questions.explanation: When light is no longer the limiting factor, another factor (such as CO2 concentration or temperature) becomes the bottleneck. Even with abundant light, if CO2 is scarce or temperature is too low for enzymes, the rate cannot increase further. This demonstrates the concept of limiting factors.

questions.stem: A variegated leaf (green and white areas) is tested for starch after exposure to light. Where would you expect starch to be present?

options.text: In both the green and white areas equally
Only in the white areas
Only in the green areas, which contain chlorophyll
In neither area

questions.explanation: The green areas contain chlorophyll, which is essential for absorbing light energy for photosynthesis. The white areas lack chlorophyll and therefore cannot photosynthesise, so no glucose (and thus no starch) is produced there. This experiment demonstrates that chlorophyll is necessary for photosynthesis.

questions.stem: A student uses sodium hydroxide (NaOH) to absorb CO2 from the air around a plant. After testing the leaves for starch, they find no starch is present. What does this show?

options.text: Sodium hydroxide is toxic to plants
Carbon dioxide is required for photosynthesis
Light is not needed for photosynthesis
The plant used starch for respiration

questions.explanation: By removing CO2 from the air around the plant (NaOH absorbs CO2), the plant cannot photosynthesise because CO2 is a raw material for the reaction. No glucose is produced, so no starch is stored. This experiment demonstrates that carbon dioxide is essential for photosynthesis.
